drills.q: Is Kafka's ordering guarantee per-topic or per-partition? What mechanism actually delivers per-key ordering?
drills.a: Per-partition only, never per-topic. Per-key ordering is a side effect of hash-based routing: messages with the same key always land on the same partition, so in-partition append order preserves per-key order. There is no cross-partition ordering guarantee.

drills.q: Define consumer lag. What does a linearly climbing lag indicate versus one partition's lag being far above the group average?
drills.a: Lag = latest_offset - committed_offset. Linearly climbing lag across the group indicates sustained under-capacity (slow processing or too few consumers for the throughput). One partition's lag far above the average indicates key skew -- a hot key concentrated on that partition -- which adding more consumers does not fix.

drills.q: What is Kafka's default log retention, and how does cleanup.policy=compact differ from the default delete policy?
drills.a: Default retention is 168 hours (7 days) under cleanup.policy=delete, which discards whole segments past that age. Compact instead retains only the latest value per key regardless of age, turning the topic into a durable snapshot of current state rather than a time-bounded event history.

drills.q: State precisely what Kafka's exactly-once semantics guarantees, and identify the boundary where it stops applying.
drills.a: The idempotent producer deduplicates retried sends (via producer-id + sequence number) and transactions make multi-partition writes plus offset commits atomic, giving effectively-once processing entirely within Kafka's own write/read path. It stops applying the instant a consumer's processing has a side effect outside Kafka (a DB write, an API call) -- that boundary is back to at-least-once and needs its own idempotency mechanism.

drills.q: Explain the difference between eager and cooperative consumer group rebalancing, and name the KIP and default assignor for the fix.
drills.a: Eager rebalancing is stop-the-world: all consumers revoke every partition and the group pauses until reassignment completes, even for unaffected consumers. Cooperative rebalancing (KIP-429, CooperativeStickyAssignor) is incremental and two-phase, revoking only the partitions actually moving while unaffected consumers keep processing.

drills.q: A tombstone was written to a compacted topic 3 days ago with delete.retention.ms at its default. A consumer does a fresh replay from the beginning today. Does it see the tombstone?
drills.a: No. The default delete.retention.ms is 24 hours; past that window the tombstone is physically removed during compaction. The key is simply absent from the replay -- there's no tombstone left to observe, so 'seeing a tombstone' only works for consumers reading continuously within the retention window.

drills.q: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve, and what specific mechanism does Debezium use to relay outbox events to Kafka?
drills.a: It solves the dual-write problem: an app writing to its own DB and separately publishing to a broker has no atomicity between the two operations. The outbox pattern writes an outbox row in the same DB transaction as the business data (making it atomic by construction), and Debezium reads the database's transaction log directly (binlog/WAL), not by polling the table, to relay those changes to Kafka in near real time with zero extra load on the table.

drills.q: Distinguish tumbling, hopping, and session windows, and give a case where session windows are the only correct choice.
drills.a: Tumbling: fixed-size, non-overlapping. Hopping: fixed-size, overlapping (advance step smaller than window size). Session: bounded by a gap of inactivity rather than a fixed clock. Session windows are correct when the natural grouping boundary is a behavioral gap, e.g. grouping a user's clickstream into browsing sessions defined by 30 minutes of inactivity -- a clock-based window would arbitrarily cut a continuous session at a boundary with no relationship to actual behavior.

drills.q: Why does stream processing need watermarks when batch processing has no equivalent concept?
drills.a: A batch job's input is complete and bounded by definition, so there's no ambiguity about when an aggregation is final. A streaming job's input never definitively ends and records can arrive late relative to their event time; a watermark is the explicit policy for how long to wait for stragglers before considering a window closed, an accuracy-vs-latency tradeoff that simply doesn't exist when the dataset is already complete.

drills.q: A customer reports a duplicate charge despite the producer having idempotence enabled. Where do you look, and why doesn't producer idempotence prevent this?
drills.a: Look at the consumer's side effect boundary (the payment API call). The idempotent producer only deduplicates retried sends from producer to broker via producer-id and sequence number -- it has nothing to do with what a consumer does downstream. The likely cause: the consumer called the payment API, then crashed before committing its offset, so on restart it legitimately re-read the same message (at-least-once redelivery) and called the payment API again with no idempotency key on that call.

drills.q: Design the partitioning key for an order-processing topic where one customer generates 40% of orders and per-order-id sequencing (not per-customer) is the actual ordering requirement. What key do you choose and why?
drills.a: Partition by order_id, not customer_id. Since the ordering requirement is per-order (a single order's state transitions must be sequential), keying by order_id spreads the heavy customer's orders across partitions via independent hashes, avoiding the key-skew hotspot that keying by customer_id would create, while still satisfying the actual ordering requirement.

drills.q: Compare Kafka's and Pulsar's storage architecture and state the concrete operational tradeoff Pulsar's design accepts in exchange for its benefits.
drills.a: Kafka couples compute (broker) and storage (local partition segments on the broker's disk) in one process. Pulsar separates them: stateless brokers handle routing while a separate distributed log layer (BookKeeper) holds the data, enabling independent scaling of compute vs storage and native tiered storage. The tradeoff: Pulsar requires operating two distributed systems (brokers and BookKeeper) instead of one, which is genuinely more operational complexity than Kafka for teams that don't need the independent-scaling property.
